messages.text:
finish implementing .agents/plans/bifrost-native-resolution-engine.md

I'm in a hurry, so parallelize what you can.

  Also: remember that builds here are SLOW, it's fucking rust and it's over 1M sloc. The more work you can reasonably get done
  between build and test cycles, the more efficient it will be, obviously there are diminishing returns in extremis so don't be
  ridiculous, just use good judgement.

The argument-independent binding change and its schema migration are ready for validation. The visibility work is using exact reference/declaration identities and canonical module context, so same-named declarations cannot accidentally share an access decision.

The shared engine now has an access-policy hook, and the Rust producer fixes retain nested `Self` references without duplicating qualified type references. The Rust policy implementation is still in progress. Once it is connected, I’ll run the integrated tests, including the mixed module/type case that exposed the last missing route.

The visibility policy is now connected to context construction. I’m waiting on its canonical fact reader and checking the migration tests in parallel—specifically that upgrading replays affected Rust data while preserving sealed, unaffected data. No cutover gate has passed yet.

The new policy tests cover the key proof boundaries: allowed access removes only visibility uncertainty, denied access removes the target, and unknown access preserves both target and uncertainty. Review also caught a context-extension bug, which is fixed. I’m checking the SQL read cost before the next build.

I added an end-to-end private-method test: calls from the declaring module and a child module must be proven, while a sibling-module call must be excluded. The SQL review is also checking for scans repeated once per reference, which could threaten the latency gate even with correct answers.

The SQL review confirmed a costly pattern: each reference query could scan all earlier source occurrences in its file. We’re changing that to load module contexts once per requested file. I’m also replacing declaration-range matching with exact canonical context-parent traversal.

The integrated build and broad test run are now underway. This batch includes the source fixes, binding-completion changes, schema 109, visibility policy, forward/reverse regressions, and the two SQL read changes. I’ll keep the tree frozen while it runs and review the remaining cutover work in parallel.

Compilation found integration errors in imports, test access, and collection types before the tests could run. I’ve fixed the reported errors together and am letting the remaining build jobs finish so the retry reuses their output.

The next pass is building with two more fail-closed fixes: missing module placement remains uncertain, and missing canonical visibility data is an error. Declaration context now follows exact parent links in both persisted and dirty-buffer paths, keeping their access decisions aligned.

The retry is compiling the analysis crate now, after waiting on the shared Cargo package cache. The routing audit is complete too: production still uses the incumbent Rust paths. I have the point, reverse, graph, and rename integration points mapped for the atomic cutover once the correctness gate passes.

The build is still running. A direct SQL plan check caught another issue in the reference-context query: SQLite reordered the joins into a full source-occurrence scan. I’ve isolated the join-order correction for the next batch; the declaration-parent query already uses the intended primary-key lookups.

The broader run finished: 2,390 passed and 23 failed, down from 105 failures in the earlier broad run. I’m grouping the remaining failures by cause while the SQL query-plan fixes finish in parallel. Rust production cutover is still pending.

The failures include stale fixture expectations and a completion-propagation bug: reverse lookup still retains some pre-refinement uncertainty after forward binding has resolved it. I’m working on that shared engine path; parallel workers are fixing fixture setup and checking the module-boundary cases.

A key distinction is emerging: “which declaration does this name refer to?” must stay separate from “is this invocation valid?” The new Rust rule still mixes those questions for missing names and local callable variables. I’m checking that contract before changing the shared completion logic; the invocation facts and their uncertainty will remain intact.

The binding correction is in place, including regressions for missing names, local value binders, and missing signature inventory. The SQL review also caught a full semantic-table scan at the maximum batch size; that join-order fix is being tightened before the next combined build.

The next combined test run is building. This batch includes the binding fix, typed-`self` gap locality, canonical overlay setup, privacy parity tests, and bounded SQL reader checks. I’m recording it as an unaccepted checkpoint while validation runs; production routing remains unchanged.

Checkpoint `7542328cd` is committed locally. The new parity test hit two compile errors in its setup—a constant passed to `concat!` and reuse of a consuming operation API. Both are corrected, and the combined build is running again. No production cutover or push has occurred.

The run finished with 2,336 passing and 81 failing tests. Most failures share one cause: the binding refinement removed provenance required by the publication seal. I’ve corrected that distinction—retain the raw obligation, discharge it only in the binding answer—and am checking the remaining failures before the next build.

The transient Rust authority lowering is now a separate phase, preserving the final atomic publication step and adding cancellation checks to its reference walk. The producer test also now checks the actual new call-result projection. These fixes are batched for the next combined run.

Review found another evidence bug: binding completion can be correct while the rich result loses the call’s invocation uncertainty. A worker is fixing that with exact-reason assertions. The combined build continues; production routing remains unchanged pending the correctness gates.

The corrected batch compiled in 2m43s and is running 2,417 tests. In parallel, the result-evidence fix is underway and the point/type cutover interfaces are being mapped, so preparation can continue while the tests run.

The rerun is down to 10 failures, with 2,407 passing. The publication failures are gone, and the inherent/private-member tests pass. Remaining work includes one reverse-proof failure, stale fixture/work expectations, and planner-test setup that attempted `ANALYZE` on a read-only connection.

The remaining module-prefix path was using rich type completion where it consumes a module declaration identity. I’ve switched that boundary to binding completion; the canonical module-edge check still rejects generic and other non-module targets. I’m also updating the budget laws so one run reports all changed work measurements.

The point-query trace now shows five candidate/path operations, down from six. Total search SQL is 227 statements and 207 decoded rows; cold and warm opens are unchanged. Those exact costs remain pinned, along with the budget-boundary and cancellation/retry checks.

Checkpoint `990078695` is committed locally; the combined validation is still running. It includes the provenance and result-evidence fixes and the module-prefix completion correction. No production cutover or push has occurred.

The exact invocation-evidence assertions and both planner-statistics states pass. The module-prefix change did not resolve the remaining reverse-proof failure, so I’m adding a diagnostic to identify its actual residual reason. The new budget measurements are captured and pinned; cancellation replay no longer needs broad check-count searches.

I found an ordering bug: qualified resolution checked whether the module route was complete before discharging the eligible callee’s invocation obligation. That could send a known module into nominal member lookup and create a spurious missing-scope gap. The correction moves that discharge earlier, while retaining raw cancellation evidence and mixed module/type uncertainty.

The ordering correction is ready for the combined run, which is currently waiting on another Cargo package-cache lock. I’ll keep the same package set for the following checks to reuse build artifacts.

The combined build finished in 2m01s and the 2,417-test run is underway. I’ve also added timing spans around native reverse setup, workspace-context preparation, and frontier queries for the exact-workload retry.

All 2,417 selected tests passed, including the qualified-module fix and cancellation checks. I’m running the scale checks next, then the exact missing-tests workload; production routing is still unchanged.

The tests pass, but review found two native `get_type` gaps: Rust doesn’t publish return-type properties yet, and persisted intrinsic types lose their spelling. Two workers are designing those changes while the scale run proceeds.

The 256-mount lookup returned the correct complete answer. Its old cost pin needs updating: search used 262 statements and 5,914 decoded rows. I’ll collect all three sizes before updating the pins and rerunning them together.

All three sizes returned the correct complete answer, with the same five-path lexical workload. I’ve updated the measured cost pins and started their confirmation run. The largest point search took 2.35 seconds here; that isn’t the whole-request latency acceptance.

The scale confirmation is still compiling. I’m using that time to review how native results reach public APIs, particularly where a known declaration may still have incomplete type or invocation evidence.
The 256-, 1,024-, and 2,048-mount scale checks all passed. I’m starting the exact #2767 workload now, checking for 10 candidates: 3 reached, 6 missing, and 1 indeterminate.

Checkpoint `226a68ac4` contains the tested module-binding correction and scale pins. The exact workload is running and hasn’t produced a partition yet. Nothing has been pushed or switched to native production routing.

The exact test is still importing/upgrading the existing analyzer cache; it hasn’t reached native reverse evaluation. I’ll let this attempt finish under the configured timeout. Meanwhile, the Rust producer worker is adding return-type and annotated-local facts.

I’ve added the schema change to retain intrinsic type spelling in the existing seed table; the fresh-schema check passes. The exact workload is still in cache upgrade, so there’s no native result to report yet.

The exact test timed out after ten minutes while upgrading the old 3.5 GB cache, before native evaluation began. I’m retrying the same tested binary with a fresh temporary analyzer cache. That preserves the existing cache and avoids another Rust build.

hang on the two reasonable approaches are

1. let the cache upgrade finish

temp cache is worst of both
You’re right. I’ll stop the temporary-cache run, clean up its cache, and let the normal cache upgrade finish without the test timeout.
The temporary run is stopped, and its 184 MB generated cache is deleted; it can be rebuilt. The original caches are untouched. The normal-cache run is now proceeding without a harness timeout.
The normal cache upgrade is still running. The return-type, annotated-local, and intrinsic-spelling changes are also compiling in one combined validation batch; production routing remains unchanged.

The upgrade is still doing CPU work, and the combined build is still compiling. I’m reviewing local-definition projection in parallel so valid parameter/local targets won’t be reported as unavailable just because they lack a `CodeUnit`.

Agreed. Java and Go will be the primary-agent-owned checks that the design generalizes. After those pass, Astra agents can own independent language groups in separate worktrees under `/mnt/optane/`, with me owning integration. I’ll record that sequence in the ExecPlan.

Recorded in [Milestone 4](/home/jonathan/Projects/bifrost2/.agents/plans/bifrost-native-resolution-engine.md:463), committed as `3a60e99cd`.

I personally implement Java and Go first. Then Astra—not Luna—owns each remaining language-group worktree under `/mnt/optane/`; I own review, merges and integrated validation.

Existing Rust acceptance and atomic JVM cutover gates remain intact.
is there anything we can parallelize in M2 and M3?
I’ll check what remains in M2 and what M3 can prepare safely before the cutover gates pass.

Yes. There’s more parallel work available now that the initial prefix/privacy/member tasks have converged.

For M2, I’d split into:

- **Rust producer coverage:** remaining return types, locals and `self` facts, with focused fixtures.
- **Consumer projections:** native definition/type results, followed by point/reverse/rename consistency tests once the shared result contract is settled.
- **Regression coverage:** persisted/overlay parity, cancellation and budget laws, plus investigation of failing expectations.
- **My lane:** shared engine and storage contracts, integration, and the exact #2767 workload.

For M3, we can prepare three independently owned consumer groups:

- Point/type lookup and navigation.
- Reverse references and call relations.
- Broad graph/RQL, dead code, diff and `missing_tests`.

Each group can prepare its routing changes and legacy deletions independently. **The production switch still lands atomically**, followed by validation of the integrated tree. We can inventory deletion targets and prepare fixtures during M2 without prematurely switching production.

I’d keep **3–4 implementation lanes**, with me coordinating shared-file changes and one batched Cargo build pipeline. More concurrent builds won’t help; parallel code work between builds will. The cache upgrade and final controlled latency measurement remain serial parts of the critical path.
sounds good, make it so, worktrees in /mnt/optane as for M4 pls

I’ll set up isolated worktrees under `/mnt/optane/`, assign non-overlapping M2 lanes, and keep shared engine/storage changes and integration here. M3 work will start with fixtures and deletion inventories; production routing stays gated on M2 acceptance.

The Optane volume has 253 GB free. I’m checkpointing the current unvalidated tranche so the worktrees include the pending type facts and schema changes. Then I’ll split producer work, store regressions, and consumer/M3 preparation into three lanes, with builds coordinated here.

- Store laws: failing work/budget/cancellation expectations.
- Consumers: trait-versus-impl coverage and M3 routing/deletion preparation.

I retain shared engine/storage work, review and integration. The lanes won’t launch independent Cargo builds.
